从朋友聚会上认识到求婚：跟着留学生浩和美咲，学恋爱中的日语、分寸和真心。: From meeting at a friend's party to the proposal: follow international student Hao and Misaki and learn the Japanese of dating, a sense of the right distance, and how to speak from the heart.
周六晚上，健太在自己家办了个小聚会，大家一起包饺子、喝点东西。浩是健太研究室的同: On Saturday evening, Kenta is hosting a small party at his place, where everyone is making dumplings together and having a few drinks. Hao is Kenta's labmate, and Misaki is Kenta's friend from college. Kenta brings the two of them together to introduce them. This is the first time they've met.
浩研究室的同学、美咲的大学同学，爱热闹、讲义气、说话直: Hao's labmate and Misaki's college classmate; loves a lively crowd, is loyal to his friends, and speaks his mind
中国留学生，在东京读研究生，认真、有点害羞，很会做菜: International student from China doing graduate studies in Tokyo; earnest, a little shy, and a great cook
日本人，出版社的绘本编辑，开朗细心，有时会把心事藏起来: Japanese; a picture book editor at a publishing company; cheerful and attentive, though she sometimes keeps her feelings to herself
健太和两人都很熟，用普通体。浩和美咲是“朋友的朋友”，刚见面时浩先用です・ます保: Kenta knows both of them well and uses plain (casual) style. Hao and Misaki are "friends of a friend," so when they first meet, Hao starts out politely with です・ます. Only after Misaki herself says 「敬語じゃなくていいよ」 do the two switch to plain style. This is the usual order in which Japanese people close the distance.
美咲，给你介绍一下。这是我研究室的浩，从中国来的。: Misaki, let me introduce you. This is Hao from my lab. He's from China.
朋友之间介绍人说「紹介するね」就很自然。「〜くん」用在关系亲近的同辈男生身上。「: Among friends, 「紹介するね」 is a natural way to introduce someone. 「〜くん」 is used for male peers you're close to. 「来てるんだ」 is the casual form of 「来ているんだ」, and 「んだ」 adds a nuance of "let me fill you in."
初次见面，我是浩。请多关照。: Nice to meet you. I'm Hao. I look forward to getting to know you.
就算是朋友的朋友，第一次见面也先用です・ます最稳妥。一上来就用普通体，日本人会觉: Even with a friend of a friend, it's safest to start with です・ます when you first meet. If you jump straight into plain style, Japanese people may feel you're being overly familiar. Be polite first, then relax once the other person does: that's the order for closing the distance.
我是美咲，请多关照哦。我和健太大学时在同一个研讨班。: I'm Misaki. Nice to meet you! Kenta and I were in the same seminar class in college.
原来是这样。美咲你现在做什么工作呢？: Oh, I see. And what do you do now, Misaki?
「何をしていますか」只说到「何を？」，后半句用升调留白，是很自然又柔和的问法。问: Instead of asking the full 「何をしていますか」, he stops at 「何を？」 and leaves the rest unsaid with a rising intonation, which is a natural, gentle way to ask. Asking too completely and directly can make it sound like you're filling out a form.
我在出版社做绘本编辑。浩你在研究什么？: I edit picture books at a publishing company. What are you researching, Hao?
环境方面的。我在学让水变干净的技术。: Something to do with the environment. I'm studying technology for cleaning water.
哪里哪里，还差得远。日语也还说得不好……: Oh no, I still have a long way to go. My Japanese isn't very good yet, either...
被夸时谦虚一句「まだまだです」是日本人的习惯。但说一次就够了，然后把话题接下去；: Responding to a compliment with a modest 「まだまだです」 is a Japanese habit. But once is enough; after that, keep the conversation going. If you keep putting yourself down, the other person has to keep reassuring you, which is actually tiring for them.
没有的事，说得很好啊。啊，不用说敬语啦，我们差不多同岁吧？: That's not true! Your Japanese is really good. Oh, and you don't have to use keigo with me. We're about the same age, right?
「敬語じゃなくていいよ」是日本人主动拉近距离的信号。对方说了这句，你就可以换成普: 「敬語じゃなくていいよ」 is a signal that a Japanese person wants to close the distance. Once they say it, you can switch to plain style; if they haven't, don't rush to switch on your own.
谢谢。那我就随便说啦。: Thanks. Okay, then I'll talk casually.
切换语气时说一句「じゃあ、普通に話すね」，让对方知道你接受了这份好意。不说直接换: When you switch speech styles, saying 「じゃあ、普通に話すね」 lets the other person know you've accepted their kindness. You could just switch without saying anything, but saying it out loud is more gracious and shows you care about how they feel.
哟，聊得不错嘛。浩做菜也很厉害哦，今天的饺子就是他做的。: Oh, you two are getting along nicely! Hao's a great cook, too. He made today's dumplings.
诶，真的吗？超好吃！下次想让你教我做法。: What, really? They're so good! I'd love for you to teach me how to make them sometime.
「今度〜てほしいな」是轻松地表达“还想再见面”的说法，不是正式的约定。听到可以开: 「今度〜てほしいな」 is a light way of saying "I'd like to see you again," not a firm plan. It's fine to be happy when you hear it, but don't push to set a date right away. Let the relationship move forward naturally.
嗯，随时都行。不过我是从擀皮开始做的，要花点时间。: Sure, anytime. I make the wrappers from scratch, though, so it takes a while.
「AにBを紹介する」= 把B介绍给A。聚会上说「紹介するね」，正式场合说「ご紹介: 「AにBを紹介する」 = to introduce B to A. At a party, say 「紹介するね」; in formal settings, say 「ご紹介します」
初次见面: nice to meet you (at a first meeting)
只在第一次见面时说；下次再见就说「こんにちは」或「この前はどうも」: Said only when meeting someone for the first time; the next time you see them, say 「こんにちは」 or 「この前はどうも」
日本理工科研究生的生活圈子，「研究室の先輩・仲間」是最常见的人际关系: The social world of science and engineering grad students in Japan; 「研究室の先輩・仲間」 (senior members and peers in one's lab) are the most common relationships there
大学的小班课。「ゼミが一緒だった」说明两人大学时关系很近: A small-group class at university. 「ゼミが一緒だった」 shows the two were close in college
「出版社で働く」「出版社に勤める」；介绍工作时先说行业，比说公司名更自然: 「出版社で働く」「出版社に勤める」; when talking about your job, mentioning the industry first sounds more natural than giving the company name
「〜の編集をしている」= 做……的编辑；做这份工作的人叫「編集者」: 「〜の編集をしている」 = to work as an editor of ...; a person who does this job is called 「編集者」
「環境問題」「職場環境」。介绍研究时先说大方向，对方更容易接话: 「環境問題」「職場環境」. When describing your research, start with the big picture so it's easier for the other person to respond
「水をきれいにする技術」：日语修饰语放在名词前面，再长也一样: 「水をきれいにする技術」: in Japanese, modifiers come before the noun, no matter how long they are
说自己「まだ下手で」是谦虚；说别人「下手」很失礼，要说「苦手」或干脆不说: Saying 「まだ下手で」 about yourself is modesty; calling someone else 「下手」 is rude, so say 「苦手」 or just don't say it at all
日本人很在意年龄上下，知道是同岁后就容易用普通体说话: Japanese people care a lot about who is older or younger; once they find out they're the same age, it becomes easier to talk in plain style
用平常的口气说话: to talk in a normal, casual way
这里指不用敬语、用普通体。最好等对方提出后再切换: Here it means using plain style instead of keigo. It's best to switch after the other person suggests it
「今度〜しよう」有时只是客套，要看对方后面会不会约具体时间: 「今度〜しよう」 is sometimes just a pleasantry; watch whether the other person follows up with a specific time
动词ます形 + 方 = ……的方法：「読み方」「使い方」「書き方」: Verb ます-stem + 方 = the way of doing ...: 「読み方」「使い方」「書き方」
正在……；处于……状态: be doing ...; be in a state of ...
动词て形 + る（口语里省掉「い」）: Verb て-form + る (the 「い」 is dropped in casual speech)
朋友之间说话，「している」的「い」几乎都会被吞掉，变成「してる」。用「してる」听: When friends talk, the 「い」 in 「している」 almost always gets swallowed, turning it into 「してる」. Using 「してる」 sounds relaxed and friendly; when talking to older people or your boss, go back to 「しています」. The more 「てる」 someone uses, the more relaxed they've usually become.
你现在在干什么？: What are you doing right now?
我在出版社工作。: I work at a publishing company.
名词・な形容词 + じゃなくていい；动词ない形去「い」+ くていい: Noun / な-adjective + じゃなくていい; verb ない-form minus 「い」 + くていい
这是给对方“松绑”的说法。刚认识的人说「敬語じゃなくていいよ」，其实是在说“我想: This is a way of releasing the other person from formality. When someone you've just met says 「敬語じゃなくていいよ」, what they're really saying is "I'd like to be closer to you." Accept it graciously and switch to plain style, and they'll feel you appreciated the gesture; insisting on keigo, on the other hand, comes across as keeping your distance.
不用说敬语啦。: You don't have to use keigo.
动词て形 + ほしい（+ な 更柔和）: Verb て-form + ほしい (+ な to sound softer)
直接说「教えて」像是在提要求，加上「ほしいな」就变成轻轻的愿望，对方没有压力，可: Saying 「教えて」 directly sounds like a demand, but adding 「ほしいな」 turns it into a gentle wish. There's no pressure: the other person can say yes, or just laugh it off. Use it only with peers or people you're close to; saying 「〜てほしい」 to your boss is impolite, so use 「〜ていただけませんか」 instead.
下次想让你教我做法。: I'd love for you to teach me how to make it sometime.
希望你下次还一起来。: I hope you'll come with me again.
朋友的朋友第一次见面，先说「はじめまして、〇〇です」并用です・ます，等对方说「敬: When meeting a friend of a friend for the first time, start with 「はじめまして、〇〇です」 and use です・ます, then switch to plain style once they say 「敬語じゃなくていいよ」. This works at parties, BBQs, and dinners at someone's home.
一见面就用普通体，或马上问年龄、工资、有没有对象，日本人会觉得「距離感がおかしい: Using plain style the moment you meet, or immediately asking about age, salary, or whether they're seeing someone, will make Japanese people feel 「距離感がおかしい」 (your sense of distance is off). On the flip side, if they've already said you don't need keigo and you keep using 「〜です」「〜ます」, you'll come across as cold.
美咲看到浩先用敬语、被夸后谦虚一句又把话接下去，会觉得「この人、ちゃんとしてる」: When Misaki sees Hao start out with keigo, and then respond modestly once to a compliment and keep the conversation going, she thinks 「この人、ちゃんとしてる」 (this guy has it together). Her offering to switch to plain style is a sign she wants to get closer; when Hao accepts it naturally, she feels they click, and the door to her heart opens halfway.
在日本，很多恋爱是从朋友的「紹介」开始的——朋友介绍你，等于用自己的信用为你担保: In Japan, many relationships start with a friend's 「紹介」: when a friend introduces you, they're vouching for you with their own reputation. That's why Hao arrived at Kenta's place early that day with dumplings he'd made himself, right down to rolling out the wrappers, and offered to do the dishes after the meal. Misaki said later that the first thing she noticed wasn't Hao's good Japanese, but that he remembered the name of everyone there and said 「今日はありがとう」 to each person as the party broke up. You don't need techniques to win someone over; first, be someone who won't embarrass the friend who introduced you. And when someone tells you 「日本語上手」, being modest once is enough. Don't be afraid of making mistakes. Only when you dare to speak up and let your shortcomings show do others get a chance to know the real you.
情景题：朋友介绍你认识一个日本女生，你的第一句最合适的是？: Scenario: A friend introduces you to a Japanese woman. What's the best thing to say first?
朋友的朋友初次见面，用です・ます最稳妥。第二句太随便；「申し上げます」用法不对，: When meeting a friend of a friend for the first time, です・ます is the safest choice. The second option is too casual; 「申し上げます」 is used incorrectly and is far too formal; and asking someone's age right away makes people uncomfortable.
情景题：对方笑着说「敬語じゃなくていいよ」，最自然的回应是？: Scenario: The other person smiles and says 「敬語じゃなくていいよ」. What's the most natural response?
对方主动拉近距离，大方接受并换成普通体最好。坚持敬语像在拒绝对方的好意；「お前」: The other person is reaching out to close the distance, so it's best to accept graciously and switch to plain style. Insisting on keigo is like turning down their kindness; 「お前」 is too rude.
美咲说「今度、作り方教えてほしいな」，这句话最可能的意思是？: When Misaki says 「今度、作り方教えてほしいな」, what does she most likely mean?
表达好感，想再见面，但还不是具体约定: She's showing she likes him and wants to meet again, but it's not a concrete plan yet
正式约好下周去浩家: She's officially making plans to go to Hao's place next week
要求浩马上把菜谱发给她: She's asking Hao to send her the recipe right away
「今度〜てほしいな」是轻松的愿望，说明她对浩有好感，但不等于已经约好了。可以之后: 「今度〜てほしいな」 is a lighthearted wish. It shows she likes Hao, but it doesn't mean they've made plans. He can naturally pick up the topic again later on LINE.
